summary: Proposes a revised format for the IANA IPv6 address registries, shown by examples of their then-current contents. The aim was to align the registries with the current IPv6 Address Architecture specification. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A big address book can be tidied so entries are easier to read and match the latest rules. This memo suggests a neater layout for the official list of IPv6 addresses.

questions: how to read the ipv6 address registry
subtitle: A cleaner way to organize and display the official list of IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The IANA IPv6 registries were organized using outdated terminology (Top Level Aggregation Identifiers) that no longer matched the current IPv6 addressing architecture specification.
tldr.mechanism: This memo proposes a revised registry format using standard hexadecimal IPv6 notation, clear references to the defining RFCs, and notes explaining the allocation history of each address block.
tldr.outcome: The proposed format makes the registries easier to read, more closely aligned with the IPv6 Address Architecture standard (RFC 3513), and more useful for network operators and administrators.

today: RFC 4147 is informational and has not been obsoleted. The proposed registry format has become standard practice for how IANA publishes IPv6 address allocations.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem
sections.content: RFC 4147 identifies a problem with how IANA organized its official IPv6 address registries. The registries used outdated terminology from an earlier IPv6 address architecture: Top Level Aggregation Identifiers (TLAs) and sub-TLAs. By the time this RFC was written, the current IPv6 standard, RFC 3513, had moved away from this terminology and now uses Global Identifiers instead. The registries were out of step with the standard they were supposed to document.
sections.eli5: The address book was organized using old-fashioned categories. A newer, better system had already been adopted, but the book had not been updated to match.

sections.title: The Proposed Registry Format
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a new format for the two main IPv6 registries: the overall IANA IPv6 Address Space registry and the Global Unicast IPv6 Address Assignments registry.

The new format uses a simple tabular layout with four columns: the IPv6 address prefix (in standard hexadecimal notation with prefix length, like 2001:0000::/23), the allocation status or receiving entity (such as Global Unicast or the name of a Regional Internet Registry), a reference to the RFC document that defines or justifies the allocation, and footnote numbers for additional context. The entire address space is covered in non-overlapping blocks, and unassigned space is noted as Reserved by IETF.

For example, the block 2000::/3 is allocated for Global Unicast addresses and is defined by RFC 3513. Special-use ranges like FE80::/10 (link-local) and FF00::/8 (multicast) are clearly marked with their purposes and RFCs.
sections.eli5: Instead of using confusing old terms, each address block now lists: what the block is, who it is for or what it does, which RFC explains it, and any extra notes. The format is clean and easy to scan.

sections.title: Key Changes and Design Choices
sections.content:
Several specific improvements are made over the old format:

Terminology: The phrase Reserved by IETF replaces vague words like Unassigned, making it clear that the IETF controls whether these blocks can be reassigned in the future.

Notation: Binary notation is replaced by standard hexadecimal IPv6 prefix notation (e.g., 2001:0000::/23 instead of binary digits), which is what networking tools and operators use every day. The column showing a fraction of address space is removed and replaced with direct RFC references.

History: When an address block has changed status over time (such as the Site-Local addresses in FEC0::/10, which were deprecated by RFC 3879), the registry notes explain the history in footnotes rather than cluttering the main table. This keeps the current state clear while preserving historical context.

Completeness: Each registry table now explicitly covers the entire IPv6 address space, making it obvious what is allocated, reserved, or available for future allocation.
sections.eli5: The new format drops confusing terms, uses the notation that engineers actually type, explains why each block is important by citing the RFC, and keeps historical notes separate from the current facts.

sections.title: Registry Examples
sections.content:
The RFC includes two detailed example tables showing the proposed format with real address allocations as they stood in 2005.

The main IPv6 address space registry spans from 0000::/8 (reserved) through FF00::/8 (multicast). Key allocations include 2000::/3 for global unicast (the main pool for public internet addresses), various blocks reserved for future use, link-local and multicast ranges, and experimental blocks like 3FFE::/16 (6BONE, noted as returning to the unassigned pool in 2006).

The global unicast assignments registry shows how IANA has distributed 2000::/3 space to regional registries and for special purposes. The table lists each /23 or larger block assigned to APNIC, ARIN, RIPE NCC, LACNIC, to 6to4 (2002::/16), and to documentation purposes (2001:0DB8::/32, now familiar as the example prefix in RFC 3849).
sections.eli5: The RFC shows what the new registries would look like, with real examples of which blocks are for everyday internet use, which are reserved, and which are for special purposes like testing or historical experiments.

sections.title: Security and Trust
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the security of the internet routing system depends on being able to verify that an organization genuinely controls the IPv6 addresses it claims. This verification starts with trusting the IANA registry: if you see an address block assigned to a Regional Internet Registry in the IANA registry, you can then check that RIR's registry to confirm the assignment to an actual ISP or organization.

A clearer, more standardized registry format helps this chain of trust. The RFC suggests that IANA registries should be machine-parseable (not just human-readable tables) and potentially signed with digital certificates so applications can confirm they are reading current, official data straight from IANA.
sections.eli5: When someone says they own an IPv6 address, networks check the IANA list to verify. A clearer list helps this work better, and digital signatures could make it even more trustworthy.
